approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would release additional government money beyond what was already set aside in the main budget and the later economic update.
The funding would come from the Consolidated Revenue Fund and would cover the government's day-to-day running costs, as required by the Constitution for such spending to be in a separate bill.

The bill is designed to work with the new Public Governance, Performance and Accountability framework, which has replaced older financial management laws, and includes notes about provisions that remain in effect until certain actions are finished.
Appropriates extra money for the government's ordinary annual services.
Provides the additional funding above the amounts from the original budget and the mid-year update.
Aligns the bill with the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability framework.
Includes notes about the ongoing effect of certain provisions from the old Financial Management and Accountability Act.
The government's departments and agencies that receive the additional appropriations for their ordinary annual services.

The government introduced the Supplementary Additional Estimates Appropriation Bills (No. 5 and No. 6) for 2014-2015, seeking nearly $377 million in additional funding. Key allocations include $248 million for the Department of Immigration and Border Protection for resettlement and processing delays for illegal maritime arrivals, and $48 million for the Department of Social Services for the Zero Real Interest Loans program.

The Appropriation Bill (No. 6) 2014-2015 seeks approval for $423 million in supplementary appropriations, with $412 million for the Department of Defence to cover foreign exchange movements and fund reallocations, and $10 million for the Department of Social Services to continue developing the My Aged Care gateway.
The speaker referred five appropriation bills to the Federation Chamber for further consideration at the adjournment of the House.

The speaker argued the 2015-2016 budget is fundamentally unfair, citing NATSEM modelling that nine out of ten lowest-income families lose while nine out of ten wealthiest families benefit, and criticised cuts to family tax benefits, paid parental leave, and the impact on South Australian jobs at Holden and in shipbuilding.
